---
title: "Analysis workflow"
subtitle: "From idea to repository: how an NCC analysis project is developed"
---

::: {.callout-note}
## Draft

This chapter is a first draft of the working group's preferred workflow for
developing an analysis project. It describes the *intended* flow; details
(templates, repository conventions, review rules) will be filled in as the
group agrees on them. Comment and edit freely.
:::

This page describes how an NCC analysis project moves from a loose idea to a
collaborative repository with a statistical analysis plan (SAP), analysis
code, and manuscript drafts. The workflow has four stages. Each stage has a
clear *home* (where the work happens), a clear *output*, and a clear *handover*
to the next stage.

| Stage | Where the work happens | Output | Handover |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1. Ideation | Anywhere — notes, chat, meetings | A research idea worth formalising | A short description of the question |
| 2. Formalisation | Claude chat (claude.ai / Claude Desktop) | A draft project SAP | The SAP document |
| 3. Project set-up | Claude Code, local machine | A project folder, initialised as a repository on `ncc-study` | The repository |
| 4. Analysis and writing | The repository (Claude Code + TSD + GitHub) | Analysis code, results, manuscript drafts | Submission / publication |

::: {.callout-important}
## The data rule applies at every stage

NCC data lives on TSD and never leaves it. Nothing in this workflow moves
person-level data: Claude helps to *plan*, *write code*, and *document*;
analysis code is run on TSD by a group member, and only aggregate,
small-cell-suppressed results come out. See [Data management](data-management.qmd)
and the `ncc-analysis-principles` skill for the full rules.
:::

## Stage 1 — Ideation: work freely

The first stage is deliberately unstructured. Ideas come from meetings, from
reading, from results of earlier projects, and from conversations with Claude
or colleagues. At this stage:

- Explore freely. Use any tool — chat, notes, a whiteboard, a scratch script
  on TSD against the data documentation.
- Do not write a SAP yet. The point is to find out whether the question is
  interesting, answerable with the NCC data, and not already covered.
- Keep a short note of the idea (a few sentences: the question, the population,
  the exposure/outcome, why it matters). This note is the only thing that needs
  to survive the ideation stage.

Ideation ends when someone decides the project should be formalised.

## Stage 2 — Formalisation: the project SAP

When an idea is to become a project, the work moves to **Claude chat**
(claude.ai or Claude Desktop) with the NCC skills installed. The purpose of this
stage is to pin down the parameters and scope of the project and to express
them as a **project SAP**.

1. Open a new conversation and describe the project: research question,
   population, exposure(s), outcome(s), data sources, time windows, and any
   constraints (approvals, data availability, deadlines).
2. Ask Claude to **draft a SAP**. The `ncc-sap-generator` skill produces a
   draft document with placeholders and flagged decisions; iterate on it in the
   conversation until the scope is settled.
3. Describe variables by name and definition only (codebook entries), never by
   example values — the `ncc-analysis-principles` skill enforces this.
4. Save the resulting SAP as a **Word document** (`SAP.docx`). This file is
   the main output of the stage.

### The SAP is a Word document

The SAP is kept as `.docx`, not Markdown. Word is the format the group and its
co-authors actually work in: it is easy to edit, comment, and track changes
in, and it can be shared with collaborators who are not in the repository.
Claude Code reads `.docx` files directly, so the Word document still serves as
the specification for the analysis code in later stages. Do not maintain a
parallel Markdown copy — one file, one source of truth.

### The SAP is a living document

In this workflow the SAP is not a one-off, filed-and-forgotten plan. It has two
roles for the rest of the project's life:

- **Decision log.** Every substantive decision — inclusion criteria, variable
  definitions, model choices, sensitivity analyses, and any later *change* to
  these — is recorded in the SAP, with a date and a short rationale. When the
  project is reported, the SAP shows what was pre-specified and what was
  changed, and why.
- **Engineering harness.** The SAP defines what the analysis code must do. In
  the next stages Claude Code reads it as the specification for the project:
  which datasets to load, which variables to derive, which models to fit,
  which tables and figures to produce. Writing the SAP carefully therefore
  pays off directly in the quality of the analysis code.

A SAP draft is versioned (v0.1, v0.2, …); a SAP is marked finalised (v1.0) when
the group agrees on it, and amendments after that are numbered (v1.1, …) and
listed in a change log inside the document.

## Stage 3 — Project set-up: folder and repository

With a SAP in hand, the project gets a home. This stage is done with
**Claude Code** on a group member's machine.

1. Create the project folder and copy the SAP into it.
2. Use Claude Code to scaffold the project around the SAP: the standard folder
   layout (see [Reproducible analysis](reproducible-analysis.qmd)), a `README`,
   a `.gitignore` that blocks data files, and skeleton scripts that follow the
   structure of the SAP's analysis sections.
3. Initialise the folder as a Git repository and create it under the
   **`ncc-study` GitHub organisation**. Repositories are private.
4. Add the collaborators on the project to the repository.

A suggested layout:

```
<project-name>/
  README.md             What the project is, who is involved, how to run it
  SAP.docx              The project SAP — living document, see Stage 2
  CLAUDE.md             Project instructions for Claude Code (points to the SAP)
  R/                    Analysis scripts, numbered in run order
  output/               Tables and figures (aggregate, suppressed results only)
  manuscript/           Manuscript drafts
  .gitignore            Blocks data files and anything from TSD
```

::: {.callout-warning}
## The repository never contains data

The repository is a workspace for code, documents, and aggregate results. It
must not contain participant-level data, identifiers, extracts, or anything
copied from TSD other than code, error messages, variable structure, and
suppressed aggregate results. Check every commit.
:::

## Stage 4 — Analysis and writing: the repository as collaborative workspace

From here on the repository is where the project lives. Group members work in
it with Claude Code, on branches, through pull requests.

- **Developing the analysis.** Claude Code writes and revises R scripts against
  the SAP. Scripts are transferred to TSD and run there; results (tables,
  figures, logs with no person-level content) are brought back into `output/`.
  Errors and variable structure can be brought back to Claude for debugging;
  data cannot.
- **Keeping the SAP current.** When the analysis reveals that a decision has
  to change, the change is made in the SAP first (with a dated entry in its
  change log) and then in the code. The SAP and the code should never
  disagree.
- **Drafting the manuscript.** Manuscript drafts live in `manuscript/` and are
  developed in the same repository, so text, tables, and figures stay together
  and every version is tracked. Reporting follows STROBE/RECORD (observational
  or registry studies) or CONSORT (trials).
- **Review.** Changes go through pull requests so that another group member
  sees them. Use issues to track open questions and tasks.

## Summary of the handovers

1. **Idea → SAP.** When an idea is to be pursued, describe it in Claude chat
   and draft a SAP.
2. **SAP → repository.** When the SAP draft is settled enough to work from,
   create the project folder with Claude Code and push it to `ncc-study`.
3. **Repository → results and manuscript.** Develop code and text in the
   repository, keep the SAP updated as the record of decisions, and run the
   code on TSD.

## Open questions

*To be settled by the group:*

- Repository naming convention on `ncc-study` and a standard template
  repository.
- Who approves a SAP as finalised, and whether a finalised SAP is registered
  externally.
- Branch and review rules for project repositories.
